### Problem: Shortest common supersequence {#sec-st-p2-scs}

::: {.p-statement}
Return any shortest string that has both `str1` and `str2` as subsequences.

$1 \le n, m \le 1000$. On `abac` and `cab` one answer is `cabac`, the only string of length $4 + 3 - 2 = 5$. On two copies of `aaaaaaaa` the answer is `aaaaaaaa`.

Source: [LC 1092 · Shortest Common Supersequence](https://leetcode.com/problems/shortest-common-supersequence/){.solved difficulty="Hard"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
A supersequence must write every letter of both strings. A letter that is shared, in the same order, can be written once and serve both. The most you can share is an LCS, so the shortest length is $n + m - \mathrm{LCS}$. The string is the alignment: write the LCS letters once, and write every other letter when the walk drops it.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
- **Length.** $n + m - \mathrm{LCS}(s, t)$.
- **String.** Build the LCS table. From $(n, m)$, if the last letters are equal, write that letter and step diagonally. Otherwise step toward the neighbour with the larger LCS value and write the letter you drop. Finish the leftover prefix.
- **Check.** Any shortest answer is accepted. It must have both strings as subsequences, and its length must equal $n + m - \mathrm{LCS}$.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Recursion

::: {.form-next}
`f(i, j)` returns one shortest supersequence of the two prefixes. An empty side returns the other prefix. Equal last letters put that letter after the supersequence of the shorter prefixes. Otherwise the two drops are both tried and the shorter result wins, with the dropped letter appended.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("scs", "rec")
    assert str(final) == "cabac"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: st-scs-rec
def scs_rec(a, b):
    def f(i, j):
        if i == 0:
            return b[:j]
        if j == 0:
            return a[:i]
        if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:
            return f(i - 1, j - 1) + a[i - 1]
        left, up = f(i - 1, j), f(i, j - 1)
        if len(left) <= len(up):
            return left + a[i - 1]
        return up + b[j - 1]
    return f(len(a), len(b))
```

##### C++

```cpp
string scsRec(int i, int j, const string& a, const string& b) {
    if (i == 0) return b.substr(0, j);
    if (j == 0) return a.substr(0, i);
    if (a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]) return scsRec(i - 1, j - 1, a, b) + a[i - 1];
    string left = scsRec(i - 1, j, a, b), up = scsRec(i, j - 1, a, b);
    if (left.size() <= up.size()) return left + a[i - 1];
    return up + b[j - 1];
}
```
:::

#### Memo

::: {.form-next}
The same strings, stored by the pair. Building a new string at every call is the reason this form is only for short inputs. The table below writes each letter once, at the end.
:::

```{python}

    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("scs", "memo")
    assert str(final) == "cabac"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: st-scs-memo
def scs_memo(a, b):
    memo = {}

    def f(i, j):
        if (i, j) not in memo:
            if i == 0:
                memo[i, j] = b[:j]
            elif j == 0:
                memo[i, j] = a[:i]
            elif a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:
                memo[i, j] = f(i - 1, j - 1) + a[i - 1]
            else:
                left, up = f(i - 1, j), f(i, j - 1)
                memo[i, j] = left + a[i - 1] if len(left) <= len(up) else up + b[j - 1]
        return memo[i, j]

    return f(len(a), len(b))
```

##### C++

```cpp
string scsMemo(int i, int j, const string& a, const string& b, vector<vector<string>>& memo) {
    if (!memo[i][j].empty() || i + j == 0) return memo[i][j];
    if (i == 0) return memo[i][j] = b.substr(0, j);
    if (j == 0) return memo[i][j] = a.substr(0, i);
    if (a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]) return memo[i][j] = scsMemo(i - 1, j - 1, a, b, memo) + a[i - 1];
    string left = scsMemo(i - 1, j, a, b, memo), up = scsMemo(i, j - 1, a, b, memo);
    return memo[i][j] = left.size() <= up.size() ? left + a[i - 1] : up + b[j - 1];
}
```
:::

#### Length

::: {.form-next}
The length does not need the letters. It is $n + m$ minus the LCS length from the previous pattern. This is the check you apply to whatever string the next button prints.
:::

##### Python

```{python}
#| label: st-scs-len
def scs_len(a, b):
    return len(a) + len(b) - lcs_row(a, b)
```

##### C++

```cpp
int scsLen(const string& a, const string& b) {
    vector<int> row(b.size() + 1);                     // one rolling row of the LCS table
    for (char x : a) {
        int diag = 0;
        for (size_t j = 1; j <= b.size(); ++j) {
            int up = row[j];
            row[j] = x == b[j - 1] ? diag + 1 : max(row[j], row[j - 1]);
            diag = up;
        }
    }
    return (int)a.size() + (int)b.size() - row[b.size()];
}
```
:::

#### Walk

::: {.form-next}
Fill the LCS table, then walk from the corner. A match writes one letter and steps diagonally. A drop writes the letter of the string you leave behind and steps that way. Reverse the buffer at the end: the walk reads the strings from the right.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("scs", "walk")
    assert str(final) == "cabac"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: st-scs-walk
def _is_subseq(needle, hay):
    i = 0
    for ch in hay:
        if i < len(needle) and needle[i] == ch:
            i += 1
    return i == len(needle)

def scs_walk(a, b):
    n, m = len(a), len(b)
    dp = [[0] * (m + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        for j in range(1, m + 1):
            if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:
                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1
            else:
                dp[i][j] = max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1])
    out, i, j = [], n, m
    while i and j:
        if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:
            out.append(a[i - 1])
            i, j = i - 1, j - 1
        elif dp[i - 1][j] >= dp[i][j - 1]:
            out.append(a[i - 1])
            i -= 1
        else:
            out.append(b[j - 1])
            j -= 1
    out.extend(reversed(a[:i]))
    out.extend(reversed(b[:j]))
    out.reverse()
    return "".join(out)

def _check_scs(a, b, text):
    assert _is_subseq(a, text) and _is_subseq(b, text)
    assert len(text) == scs_len(a, b)

assert scs_rec("abac", "cab") == scs_memo("abac", "cab") == scs_walk("abac", "cab") == "cabac"
_check_scs("abac", "cab", scs_walk("abac", "cab"))
_check_scs("aaaaaaaa", "aaaaaaaa", scs_walk("aaaaaaaa", "aaaaaaaa"))
assert scs_len("abac", "cab") == 5
```

##### C++

```cpp
string scsWalk(const string& a, const string& b) {
    int n = a.size(), m = b.size();
    vector<vector<int>> dp(n + 1, vector<int>(m + 1));
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i)
        for (int j = 1; j <= m; ++j)
            dp[i][j] = a[i - 1] == b[j - 1] ? dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1 : max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]);
    string out;
    int i = n, j = m;
    while (i && j) {
        if (a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]) { out.push_back(a[i - 1]); --i; --j; }
        else if (dp[i - 1][j] >= dp[i][j - 1]) { out.push_back(a[i - 1]); --i; }
        else { out.push_back(b[j - 1]); --j; }
    }
    while (i) out.push_back(a[--i]);
    while (j) out.push_back(b[--j]);
    reverse(out.begin(), out.end());
    return out;
}
```
:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
The recursive forms copy strings and are for the samples. The **walk** is $O(nm)$ time and memory, the same as the LCS table, plus $O(n + m)$ to print. The **length** is the one-row LCS, $O(\min(n, m))$ memory. $n, m \le 1000$ fits the table. Do not compare one printed string with a single expected string when several answers have the same length: check both subsequences and the length.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- Equal strings: the supersequence is the string itself, length $n$.
- No letter in common: the length is $n + m$, the concatenation of either order.
- `abac` / `cab` has a unique string of length 5, which is why the samples agree.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- Printing an LCS. That string is the shared part, not a supersequence. `ab` does not contain `cab`.
- Writing a matched letter twice. The length would exceed $n + m - \mathrm{LCS}$.
- Checking equality with one sample string. Another walk can print a different shortest supersequence. Test the two subsequence relations and the length.
:::

**Variants.** The longest common supersequence is not a different problem: a supersequence is shortest exactly when the shared part is longest. Two bracket strings, and a shortest regular supersequence of both, adds the balance to the state and is a shortest path rather than a plain grid: [CF 1272F · Two Bracket Sequences](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1272/F){rating="2200"}.
